claim: The DNS Firewall Advanced rule tier gives protections that help detect and monitor more advanced DNS threats, such as Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) or DNS tunneling, and more granular protections based on threat and web-content categories.
question: What does the DNS Firewall Advanced rule tier protect against?

values.display: Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) or DNS Tunneling
more granular protections based on threat and web-content

qualifiers.scope: Resolver DNS Firewall Advanced rule tier

evidence.quote: DNS Firewall Advanced Rule tier provides you with protections to help you detect and monitor for more advanced DNS threats (for example, Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) or DNS Tunneling) or with more granular protections based on threat and web-content (for example, gambling, social networking).

note: d13-085. Current truth after the 2024-11-15, 2025-11-17 and 2026-05-11 changes.

claim: On 2025-11-17 DNS Firewall Advanced added protection against Dictionary-based Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) attacks, which generate domain names by concatenating words from a predefined dictionary to evade detection.
question: When was Dictionary DGA protection added to DNS Firewall Advanced?

evidence.quote: Posted on: Nov 17, 2025 Starting today, you can enable Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall Advanced to monitor and block queries associated with Dictionary-based Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) attacks, that generate domain names by pseudo-randomly concatenating words from a predefined dictionary, creating human-readable strings to evade detection.

claim: On 2026-05-11 DNS Firewall added new threat and content domain categories to the DNS Firewall Advanced rule tier, and the existing Managed Domain Lists and custom lists became the DNS Firewall Foundational rule tier.
question: When did DNS Firewall add threat and content domain categories, and where do the older managed domain lists sit?

evidence.quote: Posted on: May 11, 2026 Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall now supports new threat and content domain categories, enabling you to configure DNS Firewall rules with additional granularity based on DNS threat types and web content associated with queried domains.
Existing Managed Domain Lists and your custom lists continue to be available under the newly designated DNS Firewall Foundational rule tier.

claim: On 2026-09-29 Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall support for Palo Alto Networks (PANW) Advanced DNS Security became generally available. Not examinable yet (generally available after 2026-07-15).

evidence.quote: Posted on: Sep 29, 2026 Amazon Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall support for Palo Alto Networks (PANW) Advanced DNS Security is now generally available across 32 AWS Regions, allowing security teams to detect and block malicious DNS traffic directly from their VPCs using PANW Advanced DNS Security rules without deploying separate firewalls or modifying VPC configurations.
Partner Managed DNS protections from Palo Alto Networks Advanced DNS Security (requires AWS Marketplace subscription).

note: Not examinable yet: GA after 2026-07-15. Keep out of questions.

claim: DNS Firewall filters outbound DNS queries that pass through the Route 53 VPC Resolver from applications in your VPCs; Network Firewall filters network and application layer traffic but has no visibility into queries made by the Route 53 VPC Resolver.
question: Which firewall can filter DNS queries made through the Route 53 VPC Resolver: DNS Firewall or Network Firewall?

values.display: filtering for outbound DNS queries that pass through the Route 53 VPC Resolver
does not have visibility into queries made by Route 53 VPC Resolver

qualifiers.scope: Resolver DNS Firewall compared with AWS Network Firewall

evidence.quote: DNS Firewall provides filtering for outbound DNS queries that pass through the Route 53 VPC Resolver from applications within your VPCs.
Network Firewall provides filtering for both network and application layer traffic, but does not have visibility into queries made by Route 53 VPC Resolver.

claim: A primary use of DNS Firewall is to help prevent DNS exfiltration of your data, which happens when a bad actor who compromises an application instance in your VPC uses DNS lookups to send data to a domain they control.
question: What is the primary security use of DNS Firewall?

values.display: help prevent DNS exfiltration of your data

evidence.quote: A primary use of DNS Firewall protections is to help prevent DNS exfiltration of your data.
DNS exfiltration can happen when a bad actor compromises an application instance in your VPC and then uses DNS lookup to send data out of the VPC to a domain that they control.

claim: DNS Firewall is a feature of Route 53 VPC Resolver and needs no additional VPC Resolver setup, and AWS Firewall Manager can centrally manage DNS Firewall rule group associations for VPCs across accounts in AWS Organizations.
question: Does DNS Firewall need extra Resolver setup, and how can you manage it across accounts?

values.display: doesn't require any additional VPC Resolver setup
centrally configure and manage your DNS Firewall rule group associations

evidence.quote: DNS Firewall is a feature of Route 53 VPC Resolver and doesn't require any additional VPC Resolver setup to use.
You can use Firewall Manager to centrally configure and manage your DNS Firewall rule group associations for your VPCs across your accounts in AWS Organizations.

claim: On April 30, 2024 DNS Firewall rules gained a setting that decides whether the rule will inspect (the default) or trust the DNS redirection chain.

evidence.quote: April 30, 2024 You can now decide if a DNS Firewall rule will either inspect (default), or trust the DNS redirection chain.

claim: With Route 53 Profiles you can apply and manage DNS-related Route 53 configurations across many VPCs and different AWS accounts, and you can share a Profile with AWS accounts in the same Regions by using AWS RAM.
question: What do Route 53 Profiles let you share across VPCs and accounts, and through which service?

values.display: across many VPCs and in different AWS accounts

evidence.quote: With Route 53 Profiles, you can apply and manage DNS-related Route 53 configurations across many VPCs and in different AWS accounts.
You can also share a Profile with AWS accounts in the same Regions by using AWS RAM.

claim: The resources you can associate to a Route 53 Profile are private hosted zones, Resolver rules (forwarding and system), DNS Firewall rule groups, interface VPC endpoints and VPC Resolver query logging configurations.
question: Which resources can a Route 53 Profile hold?

qualifiers.condition: Interface VPC endpoints were added 2025-04-28 and query logging configurations 2025-11-17.

evidence.quote: Private hosted zones and the settings specified in them.
Resolver rules, both forwarding and system.
DNS Firewall rule groups.
April 28, 2025 You can now associate interface VPC endpoints to Route 53 Profiles.

Today, AWS announced support for Resolver query logging configurations in Amazon Route 53 Profiles, allowing you to manage Resolver query logging configuration and apply it to multiple VPCs and AWS accounts within your organization.

claim: You can associate one Profile per VPC, and the number of resources you can associate per Profile varies.

qualifiers.condition: The number of resources per Profile varies; see the Profiles quotas.

claim: When a DNS query matches both a Resolver rule for a private hosted zone directly associated with the VPC and one associated through the Profile, the local DNS settings take precedence; for a conflicting domain name the most specific one wins.
question: Which setting wins when a VPC's local DNS settings and its Profile both match a query?

values.display: the local DNS settings take precedence

qualifiers.scope: Route 53 Profiles and local VPC DNS settings

evidence.quote: When a DNS query matches both the Resolver rule for a private hosted zone that is directly associated with the VPC and a Resolver rule for a private hosted zone that is associated to the Profile, the local DNS settings take precedence. When DNS query is made for a conflicting domain name, the most specific one wins.
